metaTitle: Palmetto Bug vs Cockroach: How to Tell (Photos)
metaDescription: A palmetto bug is a large cockroach, often the American cockroach. Photos and the checks that tell it from smokybrown, Australian and German roaches.
h1: Palmetto Bugs: What They Are and How They Compare With Other Roaches
dek: Palmetto bug is a nickname, not a species. Here is which large cockroaches it covers, how to tell them apart by the plate behind the head, the wings and the size, why they come indoors and what one in the house means.
excerpt: Palmetto bug is a nickname for several large cockroaches, including the American cockroach. Photos, the checks that tell them apart and what one indoors means.

quickAnswer.lead: **Palmetto bug is a nickname for several large cockroaches, and two checks sort them: the plate behind the head (a pale band around the edge on the American cockroach, solid dark on the smokybrown) and the wings (yellow streaks at the base on the Australian, short pads and a bare abdomen on the Florida woods cockroach).** [Texas A&M AgriLife Extension](https://mytexas.ag.tamu.edu/publications/cockroach-biology-and-management/) lists palmetto bug as another name for the American cockroach.
bullets: The American cockroach is 1 1/2 to 2 inches long and reddish brown, with a tan to light yellow band outlining the plate behind its head, according to Texas A&M AgriLife Extension.
The smokybrown cockroach is 1 to 1 1/2 inches long, depending on the source, and dark brown to black, and Texas A&M describes the plate behind its head as a solid dark color.
The Australian cockroach, 1 1/4 to 1 1/2 inches long, has a yellow-bordered thorax and yellow streaks on its front wings, LSU AgCenter says.
The Florida woods cockroach is 1.2 to 1.6 inches long, cannot fly, and can spray an oily, foul-smelling fluid that the University of Florida says is harmful to skin and eyes.
The German cockroach, only 1/2 to 5/8 inch long with two dark stripes behind the head, is the small indoor species, not a palmetto bug.
One big roach indoors is usually a stray: the University of Florida says outdoor cockroaches do not survive well indoors and that removing them is often all the control needed.

body.text: What is a palmetto bug?

A palmetto bug is a cockroach: the name is a nickname for several large species, not a separate insect. [Texas A&M AgriLife Extension's guide to cockroach biology and management](https://mytexas.ag.tamu.edu/publications/cockroach-biology-and-management/) lists palmetto bug, along with waterbug, as another name for the American cockroach (*Periplaneta americana*). [The University of Florida's guide to cockroaches and their management](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IG082) casts a wider net: it says the larger American, Australian, brown and smokybrown cockroaches, 1 1/4 to 2 inches long, are often called palmetto bugs.

body.alt: Reddish brown American cockroach seen from above on a white background, with long thin antennae, spiny legs, wings covering its body and a pale band around the edge of the plate behind its head
body.caption: An American cockroach collected indoors in Austin, Texas. The pale band around the edge of the plate behind its head, with a darker center, is the mark to look for.
body.credit: Insects Unlocked, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

body.text: [The University of Georgia](https://fieldreport.caes.uga.edu/news/is-that-a-roach-or-a-palmetto-bug/) calls the name a catch-all often applied to smokybrown cockroaches and their cousins, the American and Oriental cockroaches, and [the University of Florida's Florida woods cockroach profile](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN915) lists palmetto bug among that native species' common names, adding that it may describe any large cockroach often met around homes. Every source here that uses the nickname includes the American cockroach.

In Florida, UF lists the Florida woods, American, smokybrown, brown and Australian cockroaches, with the small German and Asian species, as the roaches most often found in and around homes. The nickname settles nothing, so identify the roach itself; [the complete guide to cockroaches in US homes](/learn/cockroaches) covers the species not described here.
How do you tell which palmetto bug you have?

Check the plate behind the head first, then the wings, then the size. That plate, which Texas A&M calls the pronotum, hides a cockroach's head from above. [LSU AgCenter's guide to cockroaches that live around homes](https://www.lsuagcenter.com/articles/page1685994523851) describes the American cockroach's as light brown along the edges and dark brown in the center and the smokybrown's as unmarked, and separates the Australian from the American by its darker color, yellow-bordered thorax, yellow-streaked front wings and smaller size.

body.title: Check the roach in a jar
items: **Size against a ruler.** About 5/8 inch or less with two dark stripes behind the head is a German cockroach or a look-alike, not a palmetto bug; 1 inch or more points to the table above.
**The plate behind the head.** A pale band around the edge points to the American cockroach, a yellow border with yellow-streaked front wings to the Australian, solid dark to the smokybrown.
**The wings.** Short wings or pads that leave much of the abdomen bare point to a Florida woods or Oriental cockroach, or to a young roach.
**The smell.** A strong, foul odor when it is disturbed points to the Florida woods cockroach.
**Where you found it.** A floor drain or basement suggests an American cockroach; an attic or fireplace, a smokybrown; firewood just brought in, a Florida woods cockroach.

body.text: If the insect does not have a cockroach's shape at all, compare it with [the insects most often mistaken for cockroaches, from ground beetles to crickets](/blog/bugs-that-look-like-cockroaches).
What does an American cockroach look like?

It is a large, reddish brown roach, 1 1/2 to 2 inches long by Texas A&M AgriLife's measure, with a pale band around the plate behind its head. [The University of Florida's American cockroach profile](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN298) describes that band as pale brown or yellow and says males are longer than females because their wings reach about 1/8 to 1/3 inch past the tip of the abdomen.

Full wings do not mean frequent flights. Texas A&M AgriLife says both sexes can fly, but [Texas A&M's urban entomology program](https://urbanentomology.tamu.edu/cockroaches/american/) says adults seldom fly and are capable of gliding, and LSU AgCenter says they can fly at higher temperatures and glide at lower ones, without naming a cutoff.

It lives below ground as much as in the yard. Texas A&M AgriLife calls it one of the most common cockroaches in sewer systems, and UF says it is found mainly in basements, sewers, steam tunnels and drainage systems, sometimes more than 5,000 in one sewer manhole. In Florida it also lives in trees and woodpiles around homes; in the northern United States, UF says, it is found mainly in steam heat tunnels and large institutional buildings.
How do you recognize a smokybrown cockroach?

It is dark all over, with no pale band behind the head. [Texas A&M's smokybrown cockroach page](https://urbanentomology.tamu.edu/cockroaches/smoky_brown/) describes adults 1 1/4 to 1 1/2 inches long, dark brown to black, with a pronotum of solid dark color and wings longer than the body in both sexes, and LSU AgCenter also says its pronotum has no distinct markings.

body.alt: Smokybrown cockroach seen from above on a blue background, glossy dark brown to black, with long wings and an unmarked dark plate behind the head; the species name is printed on the photo
body.caption: A smokybrown cockroach in a CDC photo; the label on the image spells the name Smokey Brown. The plate behind its head is solid dark, with no pale band.
body.credit: CDC (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: It needs warmth and moisture. The University of Georgia says smokybrowns prefer temperatures above 68°F, need constant moisture and may enter homes looking for water. Texas A&M AgriLife describes them as common outdoors in the more humid parts of Texas and other southern states, in mulch, palm fronds, soffits, attic eaves and tree holes, and [Clemson University's cockroach fact sheet](https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/cockroach-control/) says that along the coast they may live in trees, especially palmettos.

body.alt: Glossy dark mahogany smokybrown cockroach seen at an angle on a wooden rail, its long wings covering the whole abdomen and its spiny legs spread
body.caption: A smokybrown cockroach on a wooden rail in Jacksonville, Florida. iNaturalist, where this and the Australian cockroach photo below were posted, files both species in the genus Validiblatta; this page uses Periplaneta, the genus its CDC and university sources use.

body.text: Inside, check the attic. Texas A&M's urban entomology program says smokybrowns indoors are commonly found in attics or near fireplaces and that a leaky roof can attract them, and University of Georgia urban entomologist Dan Suiter says a leaking attic, such as one where water collects around a poorly sealed roof pipe, can work like a tree hole.
How do you recognize an Australian cockroach?

Look for yellow. [The University of Florida's Australian cockroach profile](https://ask.ifas.ufl.edu/publication/IN1088) says this species (*Periplaneta australasiae*) resembles the American cockroach but has light yellow bands on the outer edge of both front wings near where they attach, and LSU AgCenter adds a yellow-bordered thorax, a darker body and a smaller size, 1 1/4 to 1 1/2 inches. UF says adults are reddish brown to dark brown, with fully developed wings capable of gliding flight.

body.alt: Reddish brown Australian cockroach seen from above on a pale surface, with a yellow-bordered plate behind its head and a pale yellow streak at the base of each front wing
body.caption: An Australian cockroach photographed in Jacksonville, Florida. The yellow border on the plate behind its head and the yellow streaks at the base of its front wings set it apart from the American cockroach.

body.text: It is a roach of the warm Southeast. UF says it is most prevalent in Florida and the coastal southeastern states and is the most common cockroach found outdoors in southern Florida, living under bark, in firewood piles and other moist places, and in greenhouses, where it damages plants. LSU AgCenter says low temperatures limit its ability to establish outside tropical and subtropical regions unless it is brought indoors.

body.alt: Two Australian cockroaches from above on a blue background: a smaller wingless nymph with pale yellow patches on a dark body beside a winged female with a yellow-bordered plate behind the head
body.caption: A third-instar nymph (left) and an adult female (right), as labeled by CDC. UF says the nymphs have light yellow spots on the top of the abdomen.
body.credit: CDC (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: What is a Florida woods cockroach, and why does it smell?

It is a native Southeastern roach that cannot fly and defends itself with a smelly spray. The University of Florida's profile lists its other names as Florida stinkroach, skunk cockroach and palmetto bug and describes adults 1.2 to 1.6 inches long and up to about 1 inch wide, reddish brown to nearly black. Its front wings are short, leathery pads that cover none of the abdomen, and it has no hind wings.

body.alt: Dark reddish-black Florida woods cockroach seen from above on a stucco wall beside a window frame, with long antennae, short wing pads and a bare, segmented abdomen
body.caption: A Florida woods cockroach on a stucco wall in Lake Placid, Florida, annotated on iNaturalist as an adult male. Its wings are only short pads, leaving the abdomen bare, and it cannot fly.

body.text: Its defense is chemical. UF says the oily, foul-smelling secretion is harmful to skin and sensitive tissue such as the eyes and can reach from about an inch to roughly 3 feet, so this page suggests moving one with a jar and a piece of card, not bare hands. None of the extension sources here mentions palmetto bugs biting; [what is actually documented about cockroach bites](/blog/do-cockroaches-bite) is reviewed separately.

It is mostly an outdoor insect, recorded in coastal Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi and most of Florida, in tree and stump cavities, under bark, in leaf litter, in woodpiles and around the bases of palms near homes. UF says it is slow-moving, usually gets indoors by being carried in on something such as firewood, and has not been shown to commonly colonize buildings, with limited cases of breeding in attics.
What about the brown and Oriental cockroaches?

The brown cockroach (*Periplaneta brunnea*) is on UF's palmetto bug list; LSU AgCenter says it is often mistaken for the American cockroach but has a slightly darker plate behind the head and broader end segments on its cerci, the two small appendages at the tail. The Oriental cockroach, another cousin in the Georgia article, is dark brown to black, about 1 1/4 inches long and short-winged even as an adult, and Texas A&M says it does not fly. The water bug nickname has its own mix-ups, sorted out in [the comparison of water bugs and cockroaches](/blog/water-bugs-vs-cockroaches).

For the Oriental cockroach, the [photo guide to Oriental cockroaches](/blog/oriental-cockroaches) shows males and females and the checks that tell the species from American and smokybrown cockroaches.

body.text: Is a palmetto bug a German cockroach?

No. None of the sources here calls the German cockroach a palmetto bug. Texas A&M AgriLife describes a small, light brown roach 1/2 to 5/8 inch long, with two dark stripes on the plate behind the head and wings that reach the end of the abdomen, says it does not fly, and says German cockroaches spend their lives indoors.

body.alt: Light brown German cockroach seen from above on a blue background, with two dark parallel stripes on the plate behind its head and wings covering its back
body.caption: A female German cockroach in a CDC photo. The two dark stripes on the plate behind the head mark the German cockroach, which is only 1/2 to 5/8 inch long as an adult.
body.credit: CDC (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: The difference matters: Texas A&M calls the German cockroach the most prolific indoor cockroach, producing a generation in about 100 days, while American and smokybrown cockroaches take an average of 600 days just to reach adulthood. [The German cockroach guide](/blog/german-cockroaches) covers identification and control. LSU AgCenter warns that the Asian cockroach looks much like it but lives outdoors, flies strongly and is drawn to lights on buildings.
Do palmetto bugs fly?

Some do. The smokybrown flies, and Clemson says adult American and smokybrown cockroaches may fly on warm evenings; the American seldom flies but can glide, the Australian glides, and the Florida woods cockroach cannot fly at all.

The smokybrown can fly at people: Georgia's Suiter says it has been known to, that it is not harmful, and that one about to take off stands high on its legs with its antennae out. LSU AgCenter says smokybrowns are attracted to light and enter buildings through cracks at night. [Which cockroaches fly and which only glide](/blog/can-cockroaches-fly) is laid out species by species in a separate guide.
Why do palmetto bugs come inside?

Mostly for food or water, or by accident. Texas A&M AgriLife says American, Oriental and smokybrown cockroaches live mostly outdoors but may move indoors in search of food or water, and that the larger species often enter through poorly sealed doors, roof soffits or floor drains.

items: **Rain and weather.** UF says American cockroaches are rarely found in houses but that infestations can follow heavy rain, and LSU AgCenter says older homes with worn seals are especially open to invasion after extreme weather.
**Light.** LSU AgCenter says light from gaps around doors and windows attracts cockroaches and gives them a way in.
**Drains.** Texas A&M's urban entomology program says American cockroaches travel through sewer pipes and enter kitchens and bathrooms through drain pipes.
**Trees.** UF says American cockroaches also move in from trees and shrubs beside buildings or with branches overhanging the roof.
**Firewood.** UF says a Florida woods cockroach indoors has usually been carried in, for example on firewood.

body.text: The gap does not need to be big: LSU AgCenter says an adult American cockroach can fit through one the height of two pennies, about 1/8 inch (3 mm). [Each route cockroaches use to get indoors, and how to close it](/blog/where-do-cockroaches-come-from), has its own guide.
Does one palmetto bug in the house mean an infestation?

Usually not. The University of Florida says outdoor cockroaches do not survive well indoors, that people often overreact to them, and that removing these roaches from the house is often all the control needed.

Some signs point to more than a stray. Texas A&M AgriLife says seeing cockroaches in the daytime usually means there are a lot of them, and the outdoor species can settle in: Texas A&M places American cockroaches indoors near furnaces and heating ducts, and smokybrowns in attics. Young roaches matter too, because UF describes American cockroach nymphs as having only wing pads and Australian nymphs as wingless, so a nymph indoors walked in or hatched nearby. [Photos of cockroach nymphs by species](/blog/what-do-baby-cockroaches-look-like) and [what cockroach egg cases look like](/blog/cockroach-eggs) help you check.
What should you do once you know which one it is?
Keep the outdoor species out, and treat a German cockroach as an indoor problem. For the large roaches, the extension advice starts with the building and the yard.

items: **Seal the way in.** UF recommends caulking cracks around door and window frames and around plumbing and electrical lines, weather-stripping doors and repairing window and soffit screens.

**Thin the mulch.** UF says outdoor cockroaches breed prolifically in pine straw and advises only a thin layer of mulch within about a foot of the foundation; LSU AgCenter says to keep landscape mulch under 2 inches thick.
**Move wood and trim plants.** UF advises stacking firewood off the ground and away from the house, and Clemson advises pruning limbs and shrubs so they do not touch it.
**Fix leaks and fill drain traps.** Repair roof leaks, which Texas A&M says attract smokybrowns, and keep drain P-traps full of water, which Texas A&M AgriLife says forms a barrier against the sewer.

body.text: Roaches living indoors are worth dealing with: UF says cockroaches can spread diseases such as *Salmonella* and that their droppings, shed skins and body parts are allergens. [A bait-first plan for clearing cockroaches](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-cockroaches-canada) walks through the indoor steps, and [what glue traps and bait stations each do](/blog/best-roach-traps-canada) explains how a sticky trap shows where roaches travel. Any product used against them is a pesticide: follow its label.

body.title: Save the specimen
body.text: Scoop the roach into a jar with a piece of card rather than bare hands, then photograph it from above beside a ruler marked in inches and note where you found it. Your state's cooperative extension office or a pest professional can use those details to help identify it.

faqs.question: Do palmetto bugs bite?
faqs.answer: Biting is not among the problems the university sources used for this page describe: none of the University of Florida, Texas A&M, LSU AgCenter, Clemson or University of Georgia pages cited here mentions palmetto bugs biting people. Georgia entomologist Dan Suiter says the smokybrown cockroach is not harmful even when it flies at people. The Florida woods cockroach is the one to handle with care, because the University of Florida says its oily spray is harmful to skin and eyes. A separate guide on this site reviews the few documented reports of cockroaches biting.

faqs.question: Does a palmetto bug in the house mean it is dirty?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. University of Georgia entomologist Dan Suiter links sanitation problems to the small German cockroach, while the smokybrown cockroaches he describes live in tree holes and attics. Texas A&M AgriLife says American, Oriental and smokybrown cockroaches live mostly outdoors but may move indoors in search of food or water, and the University of Florida says American cockroach infestations in houses can follow heavy rain. A large roach that wandered in from outside is not, on these sources' account, a sign of poor housekeeping. Small, striped German cockroaches indoors are a different matter.

faqs.question: Why are they called palmetto bugs?
faqs.answer: No source settles it. University of Georgia urban entomologist Dan Suiter says the name may have started with the Florida woods roach, a species that can grow to about 1.5 inches and is commonly found in palm trees. Large roaches do use palms: the University of Florida lists palm trees among the places outdoor cockroaches live, Texas A&M AgriLife names palm fronds among the smokybrown cockroach's outdoor sites, and Clemson University says that along the coast smokybrowns may live in trees, especially palmettos. Today the nickname covers several large species, not one.

faqs.question: What does a baby palmetto bug look like?
faqs.answer: Like a smaller adult without full wings, with markings that depend on the species. Texas A&M AgriLife says young smokybrown nymphs are black with two white bands and white-tipped antennae, turning uniformly reddish brown as they get older. The University of Florida says American cockroach nymphs are grayish brown after hatching and reddish brown in later stages, that Australian cockroach nymphs have light yellow spots on the top of the abdomen, and that late-stage Florida woods cockroach nymphs commonly have yellow margins on the thorax. Several nymphs indoors are worth a closer look, since they did not fly in.

faqs.question: How big is a palmetto bug?
faqs.answer: Most are 1 1/4 to 2 inches long. The University of Florida gives that range for the American, Australian, brown and smokybrown cockroaches it says are often called palmetto bugs. The American cockroach is the longest of them at 1 1/2 to 2 inches, according to Texas A&M AgriLife, and LSU AgCenter records lengths up to 2 1/8 inches. Smokybrown cockroaches run 1 to 1 1/2 inches, depending on the source, Australian cockroaches 1 1/4 to 1 1/2, and the University of Florida puts the Florida woods cockroach at 1.2 to 1.6 inches long and up to about 1 inch wide. A roach under 5/8 inch is a young roach or a smaller species, such as the German cockroach.

faqs.question: When are palmetto bugs most active?
faqs.answer: At night, in warm and humid weather. Texas A&M AgriLife says most cockroach species are nocturnal, hiding by day and coming out at night to look for food. The University of Georgia says smokybrown cockroaches prefer temperatures above 68°F and are most active at night, when humidity is higher. LSU AgCenter says American cockroaches stay active around 70°F and cannot tolerate freezing, and Clemson University says adult American and smokybrown cockroaches may fly on warm evenings. The University of Florida adds that American cockroach infestations in houses can follow heavy rain.
